title: Carbon market risk estimation using quantum conditional generative adversarial network and amplitude estimation
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a quantum computing framework (QCGAN-QAE) for carbon market risk estimation that combines a quantum conditional generative adversarial network to learn future loss-rate distributions with quantum amplitude estimation (enhanced by a binary search) to measure VaR and CVaR. The authors propose generator circuit improvements (reordering entanglement/rotation stages and adding a quantum fully connected layer) and demonstrate on EU ETS data that their approach improves estimation accuracy and computational efficiency versus classical and prior quantum baselines.
methodology_description: The study develops a quantum-computing framework (QCGAN-QAE) for estimating carbon-market risk (VaR and CVaR). The pipeline first preprocesses daily EU ETS carbon price data into loss rates (negative returns), normalises them (min–max to [-1,1]), discretises into 2^8 segments and binary-encodes values into qubits. A quantum conditional generative adversarial network (QCGAN) is trained to learn the distribution of one-day-ahead loss rates: the generator is a parameterised quantum circuit (PQC) with three stages (preparation, entanglement before rotation, and rotation), augmented by a quantum fully-connected (QFC) entanglement layer; the discriminator is a classical neural network. The generator and discriminator are adversarially trained (min-max CGAN objective) using classical optimisers (Adam for the classical NN parts, COBYLA for quantum circuit parameters) and gradients for the PQC estimated via the parameter-shift rule. After training, the generated quantum state encoding the loss-rate distribution is measured using Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) combined with a classical binary-search procedure over the binary-encoded state space to efficiently locate the VaR quantile and to measure the probability mass of tail states needed for CVaR. VaR is decoded from the located quantum basis state; CVaR is computed as a discrete weighted sum over decoded loss rates for states exceeding VaR. Model evaluation uses backtesting (Kupiec likelihood-ratio test), failure ratio r, discrepancy Δr, and a DLC (difference between observed tail losses and estimated CVaR) metric. Comparisons are made against baselines including historical simulation, a classical CGAN, and a QCGAN with direct measurement.
algorithms_used: Binary search (over binary-encoded quantum state space)
experimental_setup: All quantum circuits and algorithms were implemented and simulated using Qiskit (v0.20.0). Classical parts were implemented in Python with standard data science libraries. No specific physical QPU was reported as used; circuit runtimes were estimated using assumed gate/prepare/measure times (TP+TM = 1 μs, TG = 10 ns) for timing comparisons.
dataset_used: Daily EU ETS (ECX) carbon price data from 2015-01-01 to 2020-12-31 (third-phase EU ETS). Source: European Energy Exchange / Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). Total 1,544 trading-day observations (holidays excluded).

experiment_input.features: Daily carbon price; transformed to daily rate of return R_t and loss rate y_t = -R_t
experiment_input.preprocessing: Min–max normalisation to [-1,1]; discretisation into 2^8 segments; binary encoding of segments (8 qubits per encoded value); historical condition window of N=3 days (encoded as 3x8 qubits); training/test split 80%/20% (no shuffling); outliers mitigated by normalisation; both condition and generated outputs encoded as quantum states.

steps: Compute daily loss rates from price series (y_t = - (p_t - p_{t-1}) / p_{t-1})
Min–max normalise and discretise into 2^8 bins; binary-encode each value using 8 qubits
Form conditional inputs using the previous N=3 days (condition qubits = 3 x 8)

Construct QCGAN generator as a PQC consisting of preparation (encode condition), entanglement (CNOT network, QFC introduced), and parameterised rotation layers (RY, RZ); discriminator is a classical NN

Train generator and discriminator adversarially (min–max objective). Use Adam for classical NN updates; use COBYLA for quantum circuit parameter optimisation; compute PQC gradients via parameter-shift rule where applicable; apply minibatch discrimination and train an ensemble of 10 GAN/QGAN instances to mitigate mode collapse (randomly select outputs)
After convergence, use the trained generator to prepare the quantum state representing the predicted loss-rate distribution

Use Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) combined with binary search over the binary-encoded state space (starting from the highest qubit) to find the quantum basis state corresponding to the VaR quantile (compare cumulative probabilities to 1-α) and to measure aggregate probabilities of tail states
Decode the found quantum basis state to obtain VaR; compute CVaR as discrete sum over loss rates > VaR weighted by measured probabilities
Backtest results with Kupiec test (LR), compute failure ratio r, discrepancy Δr = |r - (1-α)|, and DLC for CVaR accuracy
Compare results against baselines: historical simulation (rolling 100-day window), classical CGAN, and QCGAN with direct measurement
experiment_process.notes: Binary search reduces measurement complexity to O(log N) over the 2^n discrete states; QAE used to estimate amplitude sums for queried subspaces.

primary_outputs: Value-at-Risk (VaR) at 90%, 95%, 99% — decoded from binary-encoded quantum basis state
Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) at 90%, 95%, 99% — discrete sum over decoded tail states weighted by measured probabilities
evaluation_metrics: Kupiec likelihood-ratio (LR) test for VaR backtesting
DLC (difference between observed tail losses and estimated CVaR) for CVaR backtesting
Computation time comparisons (quantum-time estimates using assumed gate/prepare/measure times vs classical runtime), and number of training epochs to convergence

training_tricks: Ensemble of 10 (Q)GANs with random selection to reduce mode collapse

hardware_details.classical_environment: Python 3.8.10 with Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Scikit-learn

key_findings: [supported] The authors propose a combined QCGAN-QAE framework to estimate carbon-market VaR and CVaR by (i) learning loss-rate distributions with a quantum conditional generative adversarial network (QCGAN) and (ii) measuring probabilities with quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) enhanced by a binary search.

[supported] The modified QCGAN generator circuit (entanglement before rotation plus a quantum fully connected (QFC) layer) yields substantially better empirical VaR/CVaR estimation than the original QCGAN on the EU ETS dataset used.

[supported] Integrating QAE (and combining QAE with a binary search) into the pipeline substantially improves measurement efficiency and estimation of tail probabilities compared to direct measurement of QCGAN outputs.

[supported] On the evaluated dataset and experimental setup, the QCGAN-QAE model achieves faster training convergence (30 epochs) versus the classical CGAN baseline (300 epochs) in the reported experiments.

[supported] In multiple reported experimental settings QCGAN-QAE passes Kupiec backtests (for selected confidence levels) where the original QCGAN sometimes fails, demonstrating improved empirical calibration.

[supported] Empirical results (in the authors' experiments) show large reductions in estimated quantum-computer runtime relative to classical-computer runtime (authors report reductions on the order of 99.998% under their timing assumptions) and dramatically fewer training epochs.

[supported] The QAE + binary-search approach reduces the number of measurements required to locate VaR from linear to logarithmic in the encoded state-space size (authors state O(log N) behaviour) and achieves empirical runtime reductions in their experiments.
[speculative] The authors claim the framework is among the first applications of quantum computing to carbon-market risk estimation.

[speculative] The authors argue that quantum parallelism and the modified circuit architecture are the causes of the observed faster convergence and computational speedups (interpretative/theoretical claim).
[speculative] The authors suggest the approach generalises to broader financial risk estimation problems and will scale as quantum hardware (qubit counts, gate fidelity) improves.
[supported] The authors note limitations: the QCGAN-QAE performance at very high confidence levels (99%) can be degraded, which they attribute to limited qubit resolution in their encoding.
results_summary: The paper empirically evaluates a quantum-based framework (QCGAN-QAE) for carbon-market risk estimation on EU ETS data. By modifying the QCGAN generator circuit (swapping entanglement and rotation and adding a quantum fully connected layer) and using QAE with a binary-search measurement strategy, the authors report improved VaR/CVaR accuracy relative to historical simulation, classical CGAN, and the original QCGAN in many cases, faster convergence (30 vs 300 epochs), and large estimated runtime reductions under the authors' quantum timing assumptions. They also report that QAE+binary search better estimates tail probabilities and reduces measurement complexity to O(log N). The paper acknowledges limits at extreme tail levels (99%) attributed to limited qubit encoding resolution and frames the approach as promising pending advances in quantum hardware.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports very large runtime and convergence advantages for the proposed quantum pipeline versus classical baselines, but these results are based on simulated quantum experiments and assumed gate/prepare/measure timings rather than demonstrations on physical quantum hardware. Therefore the claimed quantum advantage is supported within the authors' simulation and timing assumptions but remains speculative until validated on real quantum processors with comparable problem sizes and consideration of noise/fidelity.
limitations: QCGAN-QAE performance is constrained by available qubit count; authors note degraded accuracy for extreme-tail estimates (99% CVaR) attributable to limited qubits.
Scalability is limited by current quantum hardware capabilities (number of qubits, gate ﬁdelity, coherence times) as acknowledged by the authors.
Susceptibility to quantum noise and circuit errors; authors explicitly emphasise circuit-depth and gate-count minimisation to mitigate noise, implying a remaining limitation.
QAE combined with binary search does not uniformly speed up measurements at all conﬁdence levels (authors observed increased running time at the 99% conﬁdence level in some settings).

Continuity and discretisation of classical→quantum encoding restrict resolution: the approach relies on discrete binning (2^n segments) and continuity of encoded ranges to produce valid VaR/CVaR—this imposes quantisation error and limits precision.

Dependence on hybrid classical–quantum training stability and discriminator design: training required minibatch discrimination and multiple GAN instances to mitigate mode collapse, indicating fragility of training.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Proposes QCGAN-QAE pipeline: a quantum conditional GAN to learn loss-rate distributions combined with Quantum Amplitude Estimation (with binary search) to compute VaR and CVaR, reporting improved estimation accuracy against classical CGAN and historical simulation baselines on EU ETS data.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Uses a hybrid quantum-classical training loop: a parameterised quantum circuit (PQC) generator trained adversarially with a classical neural-network discriminator; classical optimizers (Adam, COBYLA) and parameter-shift gradients are employed.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Introduces PQC architecture improvements (reordering entanglement/rotation stages and adding a quantum fully-connected layer) aimed at better expressivity on NISQ hardware and uses QAE with binary search to reduce measurement complexity to O(log N) over discretised states.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Reports quantitative backtesting metrics (Kupiec LR, failure ratio, discrepancy, DLC) showing the QCGAN-QAE approach yields closer tail-risk estimates (VaR/CVaR) and fewer backtesting failures compared to baselines in simulated experiments.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Employs ensemble training and minibatch discrimination (10 GAN/QGAN instances) to mitigate mode collapse, selecting outputs randomly to stabilise generated distributions.
contradictions: Paper claims computational efficiency and improved accuracy over classical baselines, but all quantum experiments are performed in classical simulation (Qiskit) with assumed gate/prepare/measure times rather than on real hardware, so reported timing advantages and scalability to real QPUs are not empirically validated.

The method asserts near-term applicability via PQC architectural tweaks and QAE reductions, yet relies on an 8-qubit discretisation per value (plus conditional qubits and QAE overhead); this discretisation-driven encoding and the lack of noise/real-hardware experiments undermine claims about scaling to higher-resolution or larger-scale market problems.
